definition: The original VOR design. Its variable signal comes from a radiation pattern that turns 30 times a second, which makes the signal's strength rise and fall (AM) at a time that depends on your direction.

A VOR whose variable signal is made by switching a radio signal around a large ring of antennas. The Doppler effect shifts its frequency (FM) at a time that depends on your direction. It is much less disturbed by nearby buildings and hills.
The VOR signal that ticks at the same moment in every direction, like a flash seen by everyone at once. The receiver compares the variable signal against it.
The VOR signal whose timing depends on where you are around the station. How far it is out of step with the reference signal gives your radial.
A second, lower-frequency signal carried inside the main radio signal. In a VOR it is a 9960 Hz tone, and one of the two 30 Hz signals rides on it as a frequency change.
Switching a signal from one antenna to the next around the DVOR ring, very fast, so that the signal seems to come from a source spinning 30 times a second.
The large, round metal platform a VOR's antennas stand on. It gives the antennas a clean, flat 'ground' so the signal leaves the station evenly.
The cone-shaped region above a VOR where the signal cannot be used. Flying through it, the needle swings and the warning flag appears, until you are past the station.
A bearing error caused by the station's surroundings: buildings, fences, trees or hills that reflect part of the signal. The reflected copy mixes with the direct signal and bends the course.
A wavy course: because of reflections, the needle swings a little from side to side around the correct course as the aircraft flies.

Equipment at the station that constantly checks the signal it radiates. If the bearing shifts too much or a signal weakens, it switches to a standby transmitter or shuts the station down, so no wrong guidance goes out.
